b: Massively dilated lymphatic channels in deeper tissues
Most commonly in neck and axilla in children; also mediastinum, retroperitoneum
Unencapsulated with indistinct margins — makes complete excision difficult; high recurrence rate
Histology: dilated channels lined by endothelium, separated by fibrous stroma with lymphoid aggregates
Strongly associated with Turner syndrome (45,X) — cystic hygroma of the neck in Turner patients.

b: Typically found in neck or axilla of children ; rarely in retroperitoneum
Can be enormous — up to 15 cm ; filling axilla or producing gross deformities
Composed of massively dilated lymphatic spaces; indistinct, unencapsulated margins → resection difficult

qs.q: Why is resection of cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) often difficult?
o: They are encapsulated and tightly adherent to the bone
They are located exclusively in the retroperitoneum
They are highly vascular and prone to immediate fatal hemorrhage
They have indistinct, unencapsulated margins and can be enormous
qs.e: Cavernous lymphangiomas have indistinct, unencapsulated margins, making complete resection difficult. They are typically found in the neck or axilla, not exclusively retroperitoneal.
